t: The phrase was coined in 1845 by John O’Sullivan, or, some historians suggest, by Jane Cazneau; it became popular only after Whig opponents of the Polk administration criticised it.

There was never a set of principles defining manifest destiny: it was always a general idea, and its proponents held divergent and sometimes conflicting views, from territorial conquest to the call of a nation setting an example.

It was bound up with the annexation of Texas, the Oregon boundary and the Mexican–American War, and with the removal of Native Americans from their land; critics at the time and since have condemned it as a justification of dispossession.
dyk: John O’Sullivan’s original idea was not a call for expansion by force: he expected Americans to settle new regions, set up democratic governments and then ask for admission to the Union, as Texas had done, and he predicted that even Canada would one day ask.
ev: The Louisiana Purchase doubles the size of the United States
The Transcontinental Treaty transfers Florida from Spain and extends the United States border with Spanish Mexico to the Pacific
Andrew Jackson signs the Indian Removal Act
John O’Sullivan uses the phrase “manifest destiny” in the Democratic Review, and the United States annexes Texas
The Oregon Treaty divides the Oregon Country along the 49th parallel, and the Mexican–American War begins
The Mexican Cession adds Alta California and Nuevo México to the United States
The Homestead Act offers western land to settlers for almost nothing
William McKinley annexes Hawaii and the Spanish–American War brings the Philippines, Puerto Rico and Guam

f.thinkers: John O’Sullivan, the newspaper man credited by most historians with coining the term in 1845; Jane Cazneau, whom some historians suggest wrote the unsigned editorial in which it first appeared; Thomas Jefferson, whose Louisiana Purchase set the stage for continental expansion; John Quincy Adams, an early proponent of continentalism; Andrew Jackson, who spoke of “extending the area of freedom”; James K. Polk, president during the Oregon and Mexican settlements; Josiah Strong, whose 1885 book revived the idea; Albert J. Beveridge, who defended the acquisitions of 1898
f.texts: John O’Sullivan’s 1839 article predicting a “divine destiny” for the United States; his essay “Annexation” in the Democratic Review (1845) and his editorial in the New York Morning News (27 December 1845); Thomas Paine’s Common Sense (1776); John Quincy Adams’s letter to his father (1811); Josiah Strong’s Our Country (1885); the historians Frederick Merk’s Manifest Destiny and Mission in American History (1963) and Reginald Horsman’s Race and Manifest Destiny (1981)
f.ideas: the unique moral virtue of the United States; a mission to spread republican government and the American way of life; a divinely ordained destiny; continentalism, the expectation that one nation would fill North America; Anglo-Saxon racial predominance; the Monroe Doctrine’s warning to Europe; Native peoples expected to assimilate, move or vanish
f.today: The phrase declined in use after the turn of the 20th century. Wilson used it in 1920 for a mission to lead the cause of democracy, and critics of United States foreign policy use it for interventions abroad. In 2025 Donald Trump used it in an inaugural address, the first president to do so in one.
